plain_english: If someone handed your body over to a random stranger, you'd be furious. So why aren't you ashamed when you hand over your mind to anyone who insults you, letting them mess with your head and throw you off balance?
original_excerpt:
If a person had delivered up your body to some passer-by, you would certainly be angry. And do you feel no shame in delivering up your own mind to any reviler, to be disconcerted and confounded?

XXIX[2]

plain_english:
Before you start anything, think about what comes before and what comes after. Then decide if you want to do it. If you don't think it through, you'll start with enthusiasm but quit when things get hard.

"I want to win at the Olympic Games." Fine. But think about what that really means. If it's worth it, then commit. You'll have to follow strict rules. You'll have to diet and give up treats. You'll have to train your body at set times whether you feel like it or not, in hot weather and cold. You can't drink cold water. Sometimes no wine at all. You basically have to hand your life over to a trainer like you would to a doctor. Then in the actual competition, you might get thrown in a ditch, dislocate your arm, twist your ankle, eat dirt, get beaten up, and still lose.

If you think through all of that and still want to do it, then go for it. But if not, realize you're acting like a child. Kids play wrestler one minute, gladiator the next. They blow trumpets, then act out plays — copying whatever they saw that looked cool. That's what you're doing too. One day you're a wrestler, the next a gladiator. Now you're a philosopher, now a speaker. But you're never serious about any of it. Like a monkey, you copy everything you see. You get excited about something new, then drop it as soon as the novelty wears off.
original_excerpt: In every affair consider what precedes and what follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit, indeed, careless of the consequences, and when these are developed, you will shamefully desist. “I would conquer at the Olympic Games.” But consider what precedes and what follows, and then, if it be for your advantage, engage in the affair. You must conform to rules, submit to a diet, refrain from dainties; exercise your body, whether you choose it or not, at a stated hour, in heat and cold; you must drink no cold water, and sometimes no wine—in a word, you must give yourself up to your trainer as to a physician. Then, in the combat, you may be thrown into a ditch, dislocate your arm, turn your ankle, swallow an abundance of dust, receive stripes [for negligence], and, after all, lose the victory. When you have reckoned up all this, if your inclination still holds, set about the combat. Otherwise, take notice, you will behave like children who sometimes play wrestlers, sometimes gladiators, sometimes blow a trumpet, and sometimes act a tragedy, when they happen to have seen and admired these shows. Thus you too will be at one time a wrestler, and another a gladiator; now a philosopher, now an orator; but nothing in earnest. Like an ape you mimic all you see, and one thing after another is sure to please you, but is out of favor as soon as it becomes familiar.

plain_english:
You have never approached anything thoughtfully. You never surveyed and tested the whole situation first. Instead, you act carelessly, with half-hearted effort.

Some people hear a philosopher speak—someone like Euphrates (though who can speak like him?)—and suddenly they want to be philosophers too. But first, consider what this really means. Consider what your own nature can handle.

If you wanted to be a wrestler, you'd look at your shoulders, your back, your thighs. Different people are built for different things. Do you think you can keep living as you do now and be a philosopher? That you can eat, drink, get angry, and complain just like before?

You'll have to stay alert. You'll have to work hard. You'll have to overcome certain desires. You'll have to leave your friends behind. Your servants will look down on you. People you meet will laugh at you. You'll come out worse than others in everything—job promotions, honors, court cases.

Once you've fully considered all this, then approach philosophy—if you're willing to give up these things to buy peace of mind, freedom, and calm. If not, don't come here. Don't be like children who play at being a philosopher one day, a tax collector the next, then a public speaker, then one of Caesar's officers. These roles don't fit together.

You must be one person, either good or bad. You must develop either your own reasoning or focus on external things. Apply yourself to what's within you or what's outside you—be either a philosopher or just another person in the crowd.
original_excerpt: For you have never entered upon anything considerately; nor after having surveyed and tested the whole matter, but carelessly, and with a halfway zeal. Thus some, when they have seen a philosopher and heard a man speaking like Euphrates[3]—though, indeed, who can speak like him?—have a mind to be philosophers, too. Consider first, man, what the matter is, and what your own nature is able to bear. If you would be a wrestler, consider your shoulders, your back, your thighs; for different persons are made for different things. Do you think that you can act as you do and be a philosopher, that you can eat, drink, be angry, be discontented, as you are now? You must watch, you must labor, you must get the better of certain appetites, must quit your acquaintances, be despised by your servant, be laughed at by those you meet; come off worse than others in everything—in offices, in honors, before tribunals. When you have fully considered all these things, approach, if you please—that is, if, by parting with them, you have a mind to purchase serenity, freedom, and tranquillity. If not, do not come hither; do not, like children, be now a philosopher, then a publican, then an orator, and then one of Caesar’s officers. These things are not consistent. You must be one man, either good or bad. You must cultivate either your own reason or else externals; apply yourself either to things within or without you—that is, be either a philosopher or one of the mob.
